claim: Enteric (typhoid) fever remains one of the principal bacterial causes of febrile disease in low-income countries.
source: Enteric (typhoid) fever, a systemic infection caused predominantly by the bacterium Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi), remains one of the principal bacterial causes of febrile disease in low-income countries (Parry et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parry et al., 2002

claim: S. Typhi is a distinct, monophyletic lineage of S. enterica that is exquisitely adapted to cause disease only in humans.
source: S. Typhi is a distinct, monophyletic lineage of S. enterica that is exquisitely adapted to cause disease only in humans (Roumagnac et al., 2006), characterised by a non-specific fever with malaise and asymptomatic convalescent carriage (Parry et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roumagnac et al., 2006

claim: S. Typhi infection is characterised by a non-specific fever with malaise and asymptomatic convalescent carriage.
source: S. Typhi is a distinct, monophyletic lineage of S. enterica that is exquisitely adapted to cause disease only in humans (Roumagnac et al., 2006), characterised by a non-specific fever with malaise and asymptomatic convalescent carriage (Parry et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parry et al., 2002

claim: There are an estimated 20–30 million new cases of enteric fever per year globally.
source: There are an estimated 20–30 million new cases of enteric fever per year globally (Crump and Mintz, 2010), with the majority occurring in Asia, but there is an increasingly recognised burden of disease across sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: Supported by citation to Crump and Mintz, 2010

claim: The majority of enteric fever cases occur in Asia.
source: There are an estimated 20–30 million new cases of enteric fever per year globally (Crump and Mintz, 2010), with the majority occurring in Asia, but there is an increasingly recognised burden of disease across sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: Supported by citation to Crump and Mintz, 2010

claim: There is an increasingly recognised burden of enteric fever disease across sub-Saharan Africa.
source: There are an estimated 20–30 million new cases of enteric fever per year globally (Crump and Mintz, 2010), with the majority occurring in Asia, but there is an increasingly recognised burden of disease across sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: Supported by citation to Crump and Mintz, 2010

claim: Resistance against the most commonly used antimicrobials for treating enteric fever has evolved successively over the last 30 years.
source: Antimicrobial resistance is a major global health challenge, and resistance against the most commonly used antimicrobials for treating enteric fever has evolved successively over the last 30 years.
evidence: General statement about temporal evolution of resistance

claim: Ampicillin, chloramphenicol and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole were originally standard-of-care for enteric fever.
source: Ampicillin, chloramphenicol and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole were originally standard-of-care for enteric fever.
evidence: Historical treatment standard

claim: Multidrug resistance (MDR) against ampicillin, chloramphenicol and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole began to emerge in the 1970s and 1980s.
source: However, multidrug resistance (MDR) against these agents began to emerge in the 1970s and 1980s (Olarte and Galindo, 1973; Wain et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Olarte and Galindo, 1973 and Wain et al., 2003

claim: Third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones became the most clinically reliable drugs for treating enteric fever.
source: Consequently, third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones (FQs) became the most clinically reliable drugs for treating enteric fever (Kariuki et al., 2015), and were formally advocated by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2003 (World Health Organization, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kariuki et al., 2015 and World Health Organization, 2003

claim: Third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones were formally advocated by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2003.
source: Consequently, third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones (FQs) became the most clinically reliable drugs for treating enteric fever (Kariuki et al., 2015), and were formally advocated by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2003 (World Health Organization, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2003

claim: S. Typhi isolates with acquired resistance against third-generation cephalosporins are rare.
source: S. Typhi isolates with acquired resistance against third-generation cephalosporins are rare (Hendriksen et al., 2015), but S. Typhi exhibiting reduced susceptibility to FQs, induced by sequential mutations in the gene encoding a target protein (gyrA), now dominate internationally (Emary et al., 2012; Kariuki et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hendriksen et al., 2015

claim: S. Typhi exhibiting reduced susceptibility to FQs, induced by sequential mutations in gyrA, now dominate internationally.
source: S. Typhi isolates with acquired resistance against third-generation cephalosporins are rare (Hendriksen et al., 2015), but S. Typhi exhibiting reduced susceptibility to FQs, induced by sequential mutations in the gene encoding a target protein (gyrA), now dominate internationally (Emary et al., 2012; Kariuki et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Emary et al., 2012 and Kariuki et al., 2010

claim: The global ascendency of S. Typhi strains with reduced susceptibility to FQs has been partly catalysed by the dissemination of a specific MDR lineage (H58) across Asia and Africa.
source: The global ascendency of S. Typhi strains with reduced susceptibility to FQs has been partly catalysed by the dissemination of a specific MDR lineage (H58) across Asia and Africa (Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2015

claim: H58 strains are rapidly displacing other lineages.
source: These H58 strains are rapidly displacing other lineages, and strains with gyrA mutations may have a fitness advantage, even in the absence of antimicrobial exposure (Baker et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker et al., 2013

claim: Strains with gyrA mutations may have a fitness advantage, even in the absence of antimicrobial exposure.
source: These H58 strains are rapidly displacing other lineages, and strains with gyrA mutations may have a fitness advantage, even in the absence of antimicrobial exposure (Baker et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker et al., 2013

claim: Protracted fever clearance times (FCTs) are associated with organisms with higher Minimum Inhibitory Concentrations (MIC) against FQs in enteric fever patients treated with ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin.
source: We have previously shown that protracted fever clearance times (FCTs) are associated with organisms with higher Minimum Inhibitory Concentrations (MIC) against FQs in enteric fever patients treated with ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin (Parry et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parry et al., 2011

claim: The fourth-generation FQ, gatifloxacin, has remained efficacious for uncomplicated disease, even in patients infected with S. Typhi strains with reduced ciprofloxacin susceptibility (MIC ≥0.125 μg/mL).
source: However, whilst the clinical efficacy of the older FQs in enteric fever is contentious, we have shown that the fourth-generation FQ, gatifloxacin, has remained efficacious for uncomplicated disease, even in patients infected with S. Typhi strains with reduced ciprofloxacin susceptibility (MIC ≥0.125 μg/mL) (Pandit et al., 2007; Koirala et al., 2013; Arjyal et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pandit et al., 2007; Koirala et al., 2013; Arjyal et al., 2011

claim: During a recent randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing ceftriaxone and gatifloxacin, conducted in Nepal, an increased number of treatment failures associated with FQ-resistant (ciprofloxacin MIC>32 μg/ml) S. Typhi was observed.
source: During a recent randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing ceftriaxone and gatifloxacin, conducted in Nepal, we observed an increased number of treatment failures associated with FQ-resistant (ciprofloxacin MIC>32 μg/ml) S. Typhi, prompting the data safety and monitoring board to stop the trial (Arjyal et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arjyal et al., 2016

claim: The data safety and monitoring board stopped the trial due to increased treatment failures.
source: During a recent randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing ceftriaxone and gatifloxacin, conducted in Nepal, we observed an increased number of treatment failures associated with FQ-resistant (ciprofloxacin MIC>32 μg/ml) S. Typhi, prompting the data safety and monitoring board to stop the trial (Arjyal et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arjyal et al., 2016

claim: 78 S. Typhi isolates were genome sequenced from the RCT.
source: We performed WGS on the 78 available S. Typhi isolates from patients in both RCT treatment arms (gatifloxacin and ceftriaxone) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure

claim: The majority of isolates (65/78; 83.3%) fell within the H58 lineage.
source: The resulting phylogeny, which incorporated reference sequence CT18, indicated that the majority of isolates (65/78; 83.3%) fell within the H58 lineage, while the remaining 13 (16.7%) represented eight different lineages (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 1

claim: 13 isolates (16.7%) represented eight different lineages.
source: The resulting phylogeny, which incorporated reference sequence CT18, indicated that the majority of isolates (65/78; 83.3%) fell within the H58 lineage, while the remaining 13 (16.7%) represented eight different lineages (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 1

claim: All but four of the H58 strains contained the common DNA gyrase (gyrA) mutation in codon 83 (S83F), which confers reduced susceptibility to FQs (ciprofloxacin MIC; 0.125–0.5 μg/ml).
source: All but four of the H58 strains contained the common DNA gyrase (gyrA) mutation in codon 83 (S83F), which confers reduced susceptibility to FQs (ciprofloxacin MIC; 0.125–0 5 μg/ml) (Parry et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by genomic data and citation to Parry et al., 2010

claim: An H58 subclade comprised of 12 isolates contained the S83F gyrA mutation, a mutation in gyrA at codon 87 (D87N), and an additional mutation in the topoisomerase gene, parC (S80I) (H58 triple mutant).
source: Nested within the S83F H58 group, but separated from the rest of the group by a branch defined by 30 SNPs, was an H58 subclade comprised of 12 isolates containing the S83F gyrA mutation, a mutation in gyrA at codon 87 (D87N), and an additional mutation in the topoisomerase gene, parC (S80I) (H58 triple mutant).
evidence: Supported by genomic sequencing data

claim: The H58 triple mutant subclade is separated from the rest of the H58 group by a branch defined by 30 SNPs.
source: Nested within the S83F H58 group, but separated from the rest of the group by a branch defined by 30 SNPs, was an H58 subclade comprised of 12 isolates containing the S83F gyrA mutation, a mutation in gyrA at codon 87 (D87N), and an additional mutation in the topoisomerase gene, parC (S80I) (H58 triple mutant).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis

claim: H58 triple mutants shared high MICs against ciprofloxacin (≥24 μg/ml).
source: Notably, these H58 triple mutants shared high MICs against ciprofloxacin (≥24 μg/ml).
evidence: Supported by antimicrobial susceptibility testing data

claim: Two non-H58 RCT isolates with ciprofloxacin MIC≥24 μg/ml had the S83F gyrA mutation, an alternative mutation at codon 87 (D87V), the S80I parC mutation, and an A364V mutation in parE.
source: Further, an additional two non-H58 RCT isolates with ciprofloxacin MIC≥24 μg/ml had the S83F gyrA mutation, an alternative mutation at codon 87 (D87V), the S80I parC mutation, and an A364V mutation in parE (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by genomic sequencing and MIC data shown in Figure 1

claim: None of the sequenced isolates harboured plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance genes (PMQR).
source: Notably, none of the sequenced isolates harboured plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance genes (PMQR) or contained additional antimicrobial resistance genes within the well-described S. Typhi-associated IncH1 family of plasmids.
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis

claim: None of the sequenced isolates contained additional antimicrobial resistance genes within the well-described S. Typhi-associated IncH1 family of plasmids.
source: Notably, none of the sequenced isolates harboured plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance genes (PMQR) or contained additional antimicrobial resistance genes within the well-described S. Typhi-associated IncH1 family of plasmids.
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis

claim: There were no significant differences in demographics between those infected with an H58 S. Typhi isolate or a non-H58 isolate.
source: We found no significant differences in demographics and no association between disease severity at presentation between those infected with an H58 S. Typhi isolate or a non-H58 isolate (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of clinical data

claim: There was no association between disease severity at presentation between those infected with an H58 S. Typhi isolate or a non-H58 isolate.
source: We found no significant differences in demographics and no association between disease severity at presentation between those infected with an H58 S. Typhi isolate or a non-H58 isolate (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of clinical data

claim: There were no differences in disease severity or demographics on presentation between patients stratified by ciprofloxacin susceptibility, except that FQ-resistant S. Typhi were more frequently isolated from adults.
source: Next, we compared the baseline characteristics of patients stratified by ciprofloxacin susceptibility (susceptible, intermediate and resistant), and found no differences in disease severity or demographics on presentation; the only exception being that FQ-resistant S. Typhi were more frequently isolated from adults (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of clinical data

claim: A significantly lower proportion of H58 S. Typhi (4/65; 6.2%) were susceptible to FQs compared to non-H58 isolates (6/13; 46%) (p=0.001).
source: A significantly lower proportion of H58 S. Typhi (4/65; 6.2%) were susceptible to FQs compared to non-H58 isolates (6/13; 46%) (p=0.001) (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Table 1

claim: H58 isolates had significantly higher (but not resistant) MICs against the majority of tested antimicrobials than non-H58 isolates.
source: and, overall, H58 isolates had significantly higher (but not resistant) MICs against the majority of tested antimicrobials than non-H58 isolates (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by MIC data shown in Table 1

claim: Treatment failure with H58 S. Typhi was significantly less common in the ceftriaxone group (3/31; 9.7%) than the gatifloxacin group (15/34; 44.1%) (Hazard Ratio (HR) of time to failure 0.19, 95%CI 0.05–0.56, p=0.002).
source: Treatment failure with H58 S. Typhi was significantly less common in the ceftriaxone group (3/31; 9.7%) than the gatifloxacin group (15/34; 44.1%) (Hazard Ratio (HR) of time to failure 0.19, 95%CI 0.05–0.56, p=0.002) (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by clinical outcome data and statistical analysis shown in Table 2

claim: There was no significant difference in treatment failure between those infected with non-H58 isolates treated with gatifloxacin (0/6; 0%) or ceftriaxone (2/7; 28.6%) (p=0.32).
source: Conversely, there was no significant difference in treatment failure between those infected with non-H58 isolates treated with gatifloxacin (0/6; 0%) or ceftriaxone (2/7; 28.6%) (p=0.32).
evidence: Supported by clinical outcome data and statistical analysis

claim: Time to fever clearance differed significantly between the two treatment groups in H58 infections, with median FCTs of 5.03 days (IQR: 3.18–7.21) in the gatifloxacin group and 3.07 days (IQR: 1.89–4.52) in the ceftriaxone group (p<0.0006).
source: Similarly, time to fever clearance differed significantly between the two treatment groups in H58 infections, with median FCTs of 5.03 days (interquartile range (IQR): 3.18–7.21) in the gatifloxacin group and 3.07 days (IQR: 1.89–4.52) in the ceftriaxone group (p<0.0006).
evidence: Supported by clinical outcome data and statistical analysis

claim: In non-H58 S. Typhi infections, FCTs were 2.87 (IQR: 2.08–3.7) and 3.12 (IQR: 2.2–4.12) days for gatifloxacin and ceftriaxone, respectively (p=0.61).
source: Again, this trend was not mirrored in the non-H58 S. Typhi infections, with FCTs of 2.87 (IQR: 2.08–3.7) and 3.12 (IQR: 2.2–4.12) days for gatifloxacin and ceftriaxone, respectively (p=0.61) (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by clinical outcome data and statistical analysis shown in Table 3

claim: In the gatifloxacin arm, H58 S. Typhi tended to be associated with a higher risk of treatment failure (p=0.06).
source: Moreover, in the gatifloxacin arm, H58 S. Typhi tended to be associated with a higher risk of treatment failure (p=0.06) and a longer fever clearance time (p=0.013) (Figure 2, Table 2 and Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: Supported by clinical outcome data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2 and Table 2

claim: In the gatifloxacin arm, H58 S. Typhi was associated with a longer fever clearance time (p=0.013).
source: Moreover, in the gatifloxacin arm, H58 S. Typhi tended to be associated with a higher risk of treatment failure (p=0.06) and a longer fever clearance time (p=0.013) (Figure 2, Table 2 and Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: Supported by clinical outcome data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2 and Table 2

claim: Those infected with FQ-resistant S. Typhi failed gatifloxacin treatment more frequently (8/10; 80%) than those infected with an intermediately resistant organism (7/25; 28%) or a susceptible organism (0/5; 0%) (p=0.007).
source: Those infected with FQ-resistant S. Typhi failed gatifloxacin treatment more frequently (8/10; 80%) than those infected with an intermediately resistant organism (7/25; 28%) or a susceptible organism (0/5; 0%) (p=0.007) (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: Supported by clinical outcome data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2 and Table 2

claim: In the gatifloxacin arm, those infected with FQ-resistant organisms had significantly higher median FCTs (8.2 days, IQR: 5.99–10.5) than those infected with susceptible (2.96 days, IQR: 2.13–3.85) or intermediately resistant organisms (4.01 days, IQR: 2.76–5.37) (p<0.0001).
source: Furthermore, in the gatifloxacin arm, those infected with FQ-resistant organisms had significantly higher median FCTs than those infected with S. Typhi with alternative FQ susceptibility profiles (median FCTs (days): susceptible, 2.96 (IQR: 2.13–3.85), intermediate, 4.01 (IQR: 2.76–5.37) and resistant 8.2 (IQR: 5.99–10.5), respectively [p<0.0001]) (Table 3 and Supplementary file 2D).
evidence: Supported by clinical outcome data and statistical analysis shown in Table 3

claim: The median FCT for those infected with an FQ-resistant organism but randomised to ceftriaxone was 3.83 days (IQR: 2.96–4.7) (p<0.0001 for the between-treatment comparison).
source: Comparatively, the median FCT for those infected with an FQ-resistant organism but randomised to ceftriaxone was 3.83 days (IQR: 2.96–4.7) (p<0.0001 for the between-treatment comparison).
evidence: Supported by clinical outcome data and statistical analysis

claim: There was a significant temporal increase in S. Typhi MICs against ciprofloxacin (p<0.0001) between 2005 and 2014.
source: There was a significant temporal increase in S. Typhi MICs against both ciprofloxacin (p<0.0001) and gatifloxacin (p<0.0001), with a sharp increase from 2009.
evidence: Supported by MIC data from 837 organisms isolated during enteric fever RCTs conducted between 2005 and 2014

claim: There was a significant temporal increase in S. Typhi MICs against gatifloxacin (p<0.0001) between 2005 and 2014.
source: There was a significant temporal increase in S. Typhi MICs against both ciprofloxacin (p<0.0001) and gatifloxacin (p<0.0001), with a sharp increase from 2009.
evidence: Supported by MIC data from 837 organisms isolated during enteric fever RCTs conducted between 2005 and 2014

claim: There was a sharp increase in S. Typhi MICs against ciprofloxacin and gatifloxacin from 2009.
source: There was a significant temporal increase in S. Typhi MICs against both ciprofloxacin (p<0.0001) and gatifloxacin (p<0.0001), with a sharp increase from 2009.
evidence: Supported by MIC data from 837 organisms isolated during enteric fever RCTs conducted between 2005 and 2014

claim: MICs against gatifloxacin in S. Paratyphi A significantly increased with time (p<0.0001).
source: MICs against gatifloxacin in S. Paratyphi A also significantly increased with time (p<0.0001); however, MICs against ciprofloxacin showed only weak evidence of an upward trend over time (p=0.06).
evidence: Supported by MIC data from 837 organisms isolated during enteric fever RCTs conducted between 2005 and 2014

claim: MICs against ciprofloxacin in S. Paratyphi A showed only weak evidence of an upward trend over time (p=0.06).
source: MICs against gatifloxacin in S. Paratyphi A also significantly increased with time (p<0.0001); however, MICs against ciprofloxacin showed only weak evidence of an upward trend over time (p=0.06).
evidence: Supported by MIC data from 837 organisms isolated during enteric fever RCTs conducted between 2005 and 2014

claim: MICs against FQs were generally higher for S. Paratyphi A than for S. Typhi.
source: MICs against FQs were generally higher for S. Paratyphi A than for S. Typhi.
evidence: Supported by MIC data from 837 organisms isolated during enteric fever RCTs conducted between 2005 and 2014

claim: The majority of the local H58 isolates (84/121; 69.4%) were closely related and represented an 'endemic' Nepali H58 clade containing a single S83F gyrA mutation.
source: We found that the majority of the local H58 isolates (84/121; 69.4%) were closely related; these strains represented an 'endemic' Nepali H58 clade containing a single S83F gyrA mutation.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis of 136 S. Typhi isolates

claim: Five Nepali strains isolated in 2013 belonged to the H58 triple mutant group and had an MIC ≥24 μg/ml against ciprofloxacin.
source: Additionally, we identified a further five Nepali strains isolated in 2013 that belonged to the H58 triple mutant group, and had an MIC ≥24 μg/ml against ciprofloxacin.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic and MIC data

claim: All the Nepali H58 triple mutants were very closely related (5 SNPs to nearest neighbour) to H58 triple mutants isolated previously in neighbouring India between 2008 and 2012.
source: Incorporating additional genome sequences from a recent international study of the H58 lineage (Wong et al., 2015), we found that all the Nepali H58 triple mutants were very closely related (5 SNPs to nearest neighbour) to H58 triple mutants isolated previously in neighbouring India between 2008 and 2012 (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4 and citation to Wong et al., 2015

claim: A new FQ-resistant subclade of H58 S. Typhi has been introduced into Nepal and is associated with a lack of FQ efficacy.
source: Our study shows that a new FQ-resistant subclade of H58 S. Typhi has been introduced into Nepal and is associated with a lack of FQ efficacy.
evidence: Supported by combined genomic and clinical outcome data

claim: This subclade was associated with longer FCTs and treatment failure in patients treated with the FQ, gatifloxacin.
source: This subclade was associated with longer FCTs and treatment failure in patients treated with the FQ, gatifloxacin.
evidence: Supported by clinical outcome data

claim: For the first time, organism genotype can be conclusively linked with a treatment phenotype in enteric fever patients.
source: For the first time, we can conclusively show how enteric fever patients respond to FQ treatment when infected with a specific subclade of H58, thereby linking organism genotype with a treatment phenotype.
evidence: Supported by combined genomic and clinical outcome data

claim: FQ-resistant S. Typhi strains circulating in Nepal most likely descended from a single ancestor carrying the triple gyrA/parC mutant.
source: Our data suggest these FQ-resistant S. Typhi strains circulating in Nepal most likely descended from a single ancestor carrying the triple gyrA/parC mutant, such as that isolated in Nepal in 2011 (Koirala et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis and citation to Koirala et al., 2012

claim: Several very closely related strains with the same combination of triple FQ resistance mutations were genome sequenced during an international study of H58 S. Typhi and belong to the same subclade of H58.
source: More significantly, several very closely related strains were genome sequenced during an international study of H58 S. Typhi (Wong et al., 2015). These organisms had the same combination of triple FQ resistance mutations as those described here; our analysis shows they belong to the same subclade of H58.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis and citation to Wong et al., 2015

claim: These strains had equivalently high MICs against ciprofloxacin and were isolated in India between 2008 and 2012.
source: These strains had equivalently high MICs against ciprofloxacin and were isolated in India between 2008 and 2012.
evidence: Supported by MIC data and citation to Wong et al., 2015

claim: This lineage was introduced into Nepal from India or elsewhere in South Asia within the last 4–5 years and has subsequently entered in an endemic transmission cycle in Kathmandu.
source: Our data implies that this lineage was introduced into Nepal from India or elsewhere in South Asia within the last 4–5 years and has subsequently entered in an endemic transmission cycle in Kathmandu.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic and temporal data

claim: Given the large extent of human movement between India and Nepal, this is the most likely route of introduction.
source: Given the large extent of human movement between India and Nepal, we propose this is the most likely route of introduction.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic data and knowledge of human movement patterns

claim: There is a small possibility that multiple strains independently gained resistance against FQs through the same selective pressure.
source: However, there is also a small possibility that multiple strains independently gained resistance against FQs through the same selective pressure.
evidence: Alternative hypothesis based on speculation

claim: FQs should no longer be used for empirical enteric fever therapy on the Indian subcontinent.
source: Our data has substantial repercussions for enteric fever treatment, and we advocate that FQs should no longer be used for empirical enteric fever therapy on the Indian subcontinent, as we predict these strains are likely to be widespread and are associated with poor outcomes with FQ therapy.
evidence: Recommendation based on clinical outcome data and inference about strain distribution

claim: Gatifloxacin binds to a different location on the DNA gyrase than the older FQs and is not as susceptible to the common resistance mutations.
source: Notably, in the RCT from which these data were derived we used the newer generation FQ, gatifloxacin, which binds to a different location on the DNA gyrase than the older FQs and is not as susceptible to the common resistance mutations (Lu et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 1999

claim: The isolates in this study were not generally resistant to gatifloxacin according to the current CLSI guidelines for Enterobacteriaceae.
source: The isolates in this study were not generally resistant to gatifloxacin according to the current CLSI guidelines for Enterobacteriaceae (CLSI, 2012); we suggest that these guidelines be modified specifically for S. Typhi to reflect these new clinical data.
evidence: Supported by MIC data and citation to CLSI, 2012

claim: CLSI guidelines should be modified specifically for S. Typhi to reflect these new clinical data.
source: The isolates in this study were not generally resistant to gatifloxacin according to the current CLSI guidelines for Enterobacteriaceae (CLSI, 2012); we suggest that these guidelines be modified specifically for S. Typhi to reflect these new clinical data.
evidence: Recommendation based on clinical outcome data

claim: S. Typhi genotyping, mapping and susceptibility testing should be performed routinely and rapidly in reference laboratories inside and outside of South Asia.
source: We additionally propose that S. Typhi genotyping, mapping and susceptibility testing is performed routinely and rapidly in reference laboratories inside and outside of South Asia to monitor the international spread of these strains and ensure the provision of alternative efficacious therapies to returning travellers (Lee et al., 2013; García-Fernández et al., 2015).
evidence: Recommendation based on study findings and citations to Lee et al., 2013 and García-Fernández et al., 2015

claim: In cases of infection with these FQ-resistant isolates, ceftriaxone and azithromycin should be used as alternatives.
source: In cases of infection with these FQ-resistant isolates, we suggest that ceftriaxone and azithromycin be used as alternatives, and do not currently recommend a return to the use of first-line drugs without contemporary data on treatment outcome.
evidence: Recommendation based on clinical outcome data

claim: A return to the use of first-line drugs is not currently recommended without contemporary data on treatment outcome.
source: In cases of infection with these FQ-resistant isolates, we suggest that ceftriaxone and azithromycin be used as alternatives, and do not currently recommend a return to the use of first-line drugs without contemporary data on treatment outcome.
evidence: Recommendation based on lack of data

claim: None of the isolates in this study were MDR.
source: Whilst none of the isolates in this study were MDR, we predict a rapid return of MDR strains if there is a hasty return to older first-line alternatives.
evidence: Supported by antimicrobial susceptibility testing data

claim: A rapid return of MDR strains is predicted if there is a hasty return to older first-line alternatives.
source: Whilst none of the isolates in this study were MDR, we predict a rapid return of MDR strains if there is a hasty return to older first-line alternatives.
evidence: Prediction based on speculation about selective pressure

claim: The RCT was conducted at Patan Hospital and the Civil Hospital in the Lalitpur area of Kathmandu, Nepal, between 2011 and 2014.
source: The RCT from which the organisms and corresponding clinical data originated for these analyses was conducted at Patan Hospital and the Civil Hospital in the Lalitpur area of Kathmandu, Nepal, between 2011 and 2014, as described previously (Arjyal et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arjyal et al., 2016

claim: Patients were randomly assigned to seven days of treatment with either oral gatifloxacin or intravenous ceftriaxone.
source: Briefly, patients were randomly assigned to seven days of treatment with either oral gatifloxacin (400 mg tablets, Square Pharmaceuticals Limited, Bangladesh) at a dose of 10 mg/kg once daily or intravenous ceftriaxone (Powercef, 1000mg injection vial, Wockhardt Ltd, India), injected over 10 min at a dose of 60 mg/kg up to a maximum of two grams (aged 2 to 13 years) or two grams (≥14 years) once daily.
evidence: Description of study design

claim: The primary endpoint was a composite of treatment failure, defined by specific criteria including FCT more than seven days, requirement for rescue treatment, blood culture positivity on day eight, relapse within 28 days, and development of complications within 28 days.
source: The primary endpoint was a composite of treatment failure, defined as the occurrence of at least one of the following events: fever clearance time (FCT) (time from the first dose of a study drug until the temperature dropped to ≤37·5°C and remained there for at least two days) more than seven days post-treatment initiation; requirement for rescue treatment as judged by the treating physician; blood culture positivity for S. Typhi or S. Paratyphi on day eight of treatment (microbiological failure); culture-confirmed or syndromic enteric fever relapse within 28 days of initiation of treatment; and the development of any enteric fever-related complication (e.g. clinically significant bleeding, fall in the Glasgow Coma Score, perforation of the gastrointestinal tract and hospital admission) within 28 days after the initiation of treatment.
evidence: Description of study design

claim: Genomic DNA from 78 Nepali S. Typhi organisms was extracted using the Wizard Genomic DNA Extraction Kit.
source: Genomic DNA from Nepali S. Typhi organisms originating from this RCT (78 isolates) was extracted using the Wizard Genomic DNA Extraction Kit (Promega, Wisconsin, USA) (Supplementary file 1) (Karkey et al., 2013).

source: Two μg of genomic DNA was subjected to WGS on an Illumina Miseq platform, following the manufacturer's recommendations to generate 250bp/100bp paired-end reads.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Time to treatment failure was analysed using Firth's penalized maximum likelihood bias reduction method for Cox regression.
source: Time to treatment failure was analysed using Firth's penalized maximum likelihood bias reduction method for Cox regression as a solution for the non-convergence of likelihood function in the case of zero event counts in subgroups (Firth, 1993).
evidence: Description of statistical methods and citation to Firth, 1993

claim: FCT was analysed as an interval-censored outcome using parametric Weibull accelerated failure time models.
source: FCT was analysed as an interval-censored outcome, i.e. as the time interval from the last febrile temperature assessment until the first afebrile assessment, using parametric Weibull accelerated failure time models (Kalbfleisch and Prentice, 2002).
evidence: Description of statistical methods and citation to Kalbfleisch and Prentice, 2002

evidence: Description of statistical methods and citations to Pandit et al., 2007; Koirala et al., 2013; Arjyal et al., 2011
